Background
The first attack was by the Thebans on the Athenian outpost at Plataea, on 4 April 431 BC. Sparta and its allies, except for Corinth, were almost exclusively land-based, and able to summon large armies which were nearly unbeatable (thanks to the legendary Spartan forces). The Athenian Empire, although based in the peninsula of Attica, spread out across the islands of the Aegean Sea; Athens drew its immense wealth from tribute paid by these islands. Athens maintained its empire through naval power. Thus, the two powers were relatively unable to fight decisive battles. The Spartan strategy during the Archidamian War was to invade the land around Athens. While this invasion deprived Athenians of the productive land around their city, Athens maintained access to the sea, and did not suffer much. Many of the citizens of Attica abandoned their farms and moved inside the Long Walls, which connected Athens to its port of Piraeus. At the end of the first year of the war, Pericles gave his famous Funeral Oration (431 BC).
Invasion of Attica
First invasion of Attica
In 431 B.C.E., a large part of the Peloponnesian military, led by Archidamus II of Sparta, entered Attica. The Peloponnesian army advanced through Attica slowly at first because Archidamus's desire was not to fight an immediate, large-scale battle with Athens but rather to create an environment in which he could coerce Athenians into capitulating to him without going to war. However, it turned out that the destruction caused by the Peloponnesian forces as they marched through Athenian territory would be worse than what the Athenians expected. After Archidamus and the Peloponnesian army reached the district of Acharnae, the Athenian public became increasingly frustrated and demanded that they confront the Peloponnesians in battle. In spite of public opinion, Pericles decided to continue his strategy of defending Attica. Eventually, Archidamus and the Peloponnesians withdrew from Attica.
Second invasion of Attica
In 430 B.C.E. (summer), the longest and worst of the early military campaigns was an invasion by Sparta which lasted approximately forty days. At the same time, the Plague of Athens broke out, killing thousands in this overcrowded urban area and ultimately killing Pericles himself. During the invasion, Spartan troops ravaged most of Attica, including rural areas as well as coastal regions all the way to the silver mines near Laurium. In contrast, the Athenians stayed behind their Long Walls and fought their enemy in direct confrontations outside the walls.
Third invasion of Attica
Sparta and its allies invaded the Attic region in the summer of 428 BC (third invasion during Archidamian phase of the war). Archidamus II led troops that ravaged Athenian farms and communities, with only limited patrols by Athenian cavalry attempting to frustrate Spartan forces. The entire population of Athens remained shielded behind the Long Walls and thus avoided a full-fledged land battle. The ultimate aim of these annual invasions was to induce the Athenians to fight an open battle; however, such strategies were ineffectual over time and especially following the Athenian Plague in 430 BC.
